strengths: Fine-tuning vision-language foundation models (e.g., CLIP) for downstream tasks is increasingly crucial and practical in today’s research landscape.
The proposed methodology is simple yet effective, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance.

The proposed method seems a very conceptually simple, computationally cheap, and easy-to-use, approach to few-shot classification that preserves all the knowledge of massive pre-training (like in the CLIP model) during training.
PEA achieved good generalization across diverse datasets, outperforming existing few-shot adaptation techniques.
The structure of this paper is clear.
The research question—few-shot adaptation of VLMs—is both well-established and of practical significance.
Experimental results across 15 datasets show that the proposed method outperforms selected baselines in few-shot adaptation and domain generalization tasks.
weaknesses: The paper appears incomplete and the overall presentation is lacking; unclear figures (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3), missing ablation study, limited experiment results, and insufficient explanations for tables/figures.

The motivation claims that large language model–based methods are ineffective yet provides no supporting experiments; lacks evidence to counter existing studies showing LLM textual enrichment improves performance.

Unclear technical novelty and differentiation from adapter‑based methods; needs detailed comparison with Tip‑Adapter and clarification of how updating image features differs from applying a learnable shift, especially given marginal performance improvements.
The reviewer suggests comparing with synthetic dataset generation approaches and discussing related works that use generative models for fine‑tuning CLIP.
In Table 2, methods not designed for out‑of‑distribution tasks are compared, making the OOD comparison unclear; suggest including OOD‑specific studies like WiSE‑FT.

The motivation section discusses text‑handling limitations but the proposed method does not address these issues; the connection between text prompt engineering problems and the PEA solution is unclear.

The rationale behind equation (6) is unclear; Δ_c in equation (5) is undefined; there is a lack of mathematical justification for the evolutionary step and the contrastive loss formulation; section 4.2 needs extensive refactoring.
The concept of a biased prototype and the role of parameter α are not explained; a dedicated section with toy experiments is needed to clarify this concept.
The mentioned ablation studies (line 393) are absent; an ablation testing the prototype approach without the evolutionary step is needed.
The text prompt used in experiments is unspecified; details should be included in the training description.
Model comparison omits recent CLIP adaptation models CoCoOp and MaPLe; a more up‑to‑date literature check is required.
Equations (1), (2), (4), and (6) contain the term x on the left‑hand side but it never appears on the right‑hand side, indicating an inconsistency.
Typo in the title: "Evoluation".
The manuscript seems not completed (e.g., insufficient results and discussion, no ablation study).
The motivation is not convincing; it lacks explanation of why dynamic prototype evolution is essential compared to static prototypes with regularization.
Inadequate description of the prototype update mechanism; shift vectors initialization, update, and regularization are not fully explained.
Excessive content about other works in the method section makes it hard to identify the novel contribution.
Hyperparameter α in equation 5 lacks detailed discussion or ablation study on its effect on model generalization.
The evaluation is not comprehensive; it lacks analysis of how PEA behaves across different types of distribution shifts.
The concept of introducing learnable shift vectors lacks novelty, as similar ideas have been explored in TaskRes, TPE, Tip‑Adapter, ProtoCLIP, and APE.
Experiments are insufficient to support the authors' claims; no experiments demonstrate parameter efficiency or intra‑class variance regulation.
Baseline results in Tables 1 and 2 appear unreliable, showing large discrepancies from the original papers (e.g., Tip‑Adapter‑F 16‑shot performance).
The proposed method is not clearly explained; it is unclear how the learnable shift vector is updated and the statement about cross‑entropy loss leading to overfitting seems contradictory.
The paper appears largely incomplete; there are no ablation experiments to validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and no accompanying text describing the results in Table 2.
Figure 1 is not referenced in the main text, and its purpose is unclear.
The caption for Figure 2 is incomplete.
It is unclear what the dashed lines represent in Table 1.
Δ_c in Equation 5 is not defined.
